sections.heading: C — Driver health, vision and hearing, and impaired driving
sections.markdown:
## C — Driver health, vision and hearing, and impaired driving

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A68
The guide lists four traits of a good driver: mindful of yourself and others, responsible for the rules of the road, familiar with how your vehicle works and takes up space, and patient and levelheaded. [A68]
Source: [A68 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A68
Practice with intent so that safe habits, such as looking over your shoulder to check blind zones, become automatic and free your attention for the changing road. [A68]
Source: [A68 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A68
Driving demands physical and mental fitness: a bad cold can slow your thinking, a headache or tight shoulders can hurt your handling, and stress can weaken your decisions, so ask a doctor about any condition that worries you. [A68]
Source: [A68 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0068]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A69
Check in with yourself before you start the engine, and if you feel unwell but still need to travel, have someone else do the driving. [A69]
Source: [A69 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A69
Washington law requires you to pass a vision test before you are issued a driver license. [A69]
Source: [A69 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A69
If your license requires corrective lenses, wear them every time you drive, and do not use dark or tinted corrective lenses after dark. [A69]
Why it matters: the lens rule has two halves, always wear them, but not tinted ones at night.
Source: [A69 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A69
Peripheral vision lets you notice vehicles and trouble from the corner of your eye while still looking ahead, and clear sight also lets you judge how far away other vehicles, people and hazards are. [A69]
Source: [A69 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A70
If night driving is hard for you, drive at night only when needed, keep your headlights on, and escape oncoming glare by looking toward the right edge of the road and steering by it. [A70]
Why it matters: the glare fix is to look toward the right edge, not into the oncoming lights.
Source: [A70 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A70
At night, keep headlights properly aimed, slow down and leave more following distance, so that you can stop within the stretch of road your headlights light up. [A70]
Source: [A70 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A70
Horns, sirens and screeching tires warn you of danger, hearing loss often creeps in slowly, and deaf or hard-of-hearing drivers can adapt by leaning more on their eyes and staying extra alert. [A70]
Source: [A70 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A70
Driving while wearing earbuds, earphones, headphones or headsets that play sound or cancel noise is illegal, although a hands-free device in one ear is allowed if it meets WAC 204-10-045. [A70]
Source: [A70 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A70
A driver holding an instruction permit or an intermediate license may not use a cell phone or any mobile electronic device while driving, not even a hands-free one. [A70]
Why it matters: the one-ear hands-free allowance does not extend to permit or intermediate drivers.
Source: [A70 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A72
Impaired driving means anything, including alcohol, drugs or tiredness, that makes it hard to think clearly, react fast or control your car. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A72
Penalties for driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs include costly fines, higher insurance rates, a suspended or withdrawn license and possible jail, and no amount of experience makes drinking and driving safe. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A72
Alcohol is the impairing substance most often involved in impaired-driving crashes, so watch for drivers acting impaired and give them plenty of room. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A72
Alcohol can make you drowsy, blur or narrow your vision, slow your reactions and scanning, make multitasking like lane keeping harder, and breed overconfidence that leads to risky moves. [A72]
Source: [A72 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A73
Never drive after using an impairing substance, never ride with a driver who has used any amount, stop friends and family from driving impaired, and arrange a sober driver ahead of time. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A73
Recreational cannabis in any form is legal for adults aged 21 or older, yet driving after using any cannabis is illegal at every age, and no amount of it is safe for driving. [A73]
Why it matters: legal to buy is not the same as legal to drive on.
Source: [A73 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A73
Cannabis can reduce attention and coordination, slow reactions, weaken car handling and distance judgment, and make you drowsier. [A73]
Source: [A73 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A74
A drug being legal does not make it safe for driving, and impaired driving is a crime whether the drug was prescribed, bought over the counter or in a store, or is illegal. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A74
Over-the-counter remedies for colds, allergies or headaches can make you drowsy, and prescription drugs, much like alcohol, can dull reflexes, judgment, vision and alertness. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A74
Do not drive after first starting a prescription, a new medicine or a higher dose until you know how it affects you, and treat any label warning about operating heavy machinery as a warning about driving. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A74
A medicine that seems harmless alone can cause severe impairment when combined with a second medicine or with alcohol, so read the warnings or ask a pharmacist first. [A74]
Source: [A74 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A75
Polydrug use, taking more than one kind of drug such as alcohol plus cannabis or medicines, can produce stronger effects than any one drug and is the most common impairment found in fatal crashes. [A75]
Why it matters: mixing substances, even legal ones, is the pattern behind the deadliest crashes.
Source: [A75 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A75
Fatigue comes from physical or mental strain, repetitive tasks, illness or lack of sleep, and like alcohol it impairs your vision and judgment and can put you to sleep at the wheel. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A75
Pull over and rest if you cannot recall the last few miles, blink often or have heavy eyelids, struggle to hold your head up, miss exits or signs, feel irritable, or drift, swerve, tailgate or hit rumble strips. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A76
Share the driving with another driver if you can, and if you are alone and getting tired, leave the road and take a 20-minute nap rather than push on. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A76
Before a long trip, get enough sleep, since most people need 7 to 9 hours, and plan breaks roughly every 100 miles or 2 hours. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A76
Feelings change behavior behind the wheel: an anxious driver may press too hard on the accelerator without noticing. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A77
To calm down while parked, breathe in through your nose and out as if cooling hot soup, or count slowly from 1 to 20 or back from 100 by threes. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A77
Aggressive driving is a traffic offense, meaning a driver purposely endangers people or property, and it is linked with speeding, tailgating, unsafe lane changes, poor signaling, ignoring traffic controls and crowding walkers or cyclists. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A78
Street racing and unauthorized street demonstrations carry severe penalties, including fines, jail and vehicle impound, for drivers and for anyone who instigates or helps. [A78]
Source: [A78 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A78
Road rage is a criminal offense: an angry reaction to a road event that turns into violence using a vehicle or another weapon, often fed by stress, tight schedules or traffic. [A78]
Why it matters: road rage moves past bad driving into violence, which is why it is treated as a crime.
Source: [A78 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A79
Signs you may be in road rage include violent thoughts toward others, speeding up to beat a light, weaving, overusing the horn or high beams, and braking or slowing down to punish another driver. [A79]
Source: [A79 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A79
If another driver targets you with road rage, move out of the way, skip honking or gestures, keep your eyes on the road, and drive to a busy place with open businesses, calling police if needed. [A79]
Source: [A79 -> src:rdmv-wa-s:washington-state-department-of-licensing:handbook:pdf-0079]

Glossary: impaired driving — anything that slows thinking, reaction or control [A72]. Polydrug use — taking more than one kind of drug [A75]. Peripheral vision — seeing from the corner of the eye [A69]. Aggressive driving — purposely endangering people or property [A77]. Road rage — anger that becomes violence with a vehicle or weapon [A78].
Memory aid: aggressive is a traffic offense, rage is a crime [A77] [A78]; alcohol leads impaired crashes, mixing leads fatal ones [A72] [A75].
